div.head: II Em 7.3
div.ab: Ðonne ðæt gedon sy, ðonne rære man cyninges munde; of ðam dæge on XXI nihton gylde man healsfang; ðæs on XXI niht manbote; ðæs on XXI niht ðæs weres ðæt frumgyld.
Ðonne þæt gedon sy, ðonne rære man cyninges munde; of ðam dæge on XXI nihton gylde man healsfang; ðæs on XXI nihton manbote; ðæs on XXI nihton ðæs weres þæt frumgyld.
Postquam hoc factum erit, erigatur inter eos pax regis; ab illa die in XXI. diem reddatur halsfangium; inde ad XXI. diem manbota; inde ad XXI. diem reddatur ipsius were frumgildum.
Ðonne þæt gedon sy, ðonne rære man cyninges munde; of ðam dæge on XXI nihton gylde man healsfang; ðæs on XXI nihton manbote; ðæs on XXI nihton ðæs weres ðæt frumgyld.

Wenn das geschehen ist, dann errichte man den Schutz des Königsfriedens; von dem Tage an in 21 Nächten zahle man Halsfang; darauf in 21 Nächten Busse für Erschlagung des Untergebenen; darauf in 21 Nächten vom Wergeld die Erstzahlung.

When that is done, then let the protection of the king's peace be established; from that day in 21 nights let the healsfang be paid; after that in 21 nights the compensation for [the killing of] the dependant; after that in 21 nights the first instalment of the wergild.

When that is done, the king’s ‘mund’ shall be established. In twenty-one days from that time healsfang shall be paid; in twenty-one days after that ‘manbot’ (the compensation due to the slain man’s lord), and twenty-one days after that the first instalment of the wergeld.

When that has been done, the king’s mund is to be established; 21 days from that day healsfang is to be paid; 21 days from then the compensation to the lord for his man; 21 days from then the first instalment of the wergild.
div.note: Twelfhyndes (Schmid's App. VII, 1) adds ‘þæs on XXI nihtan þæt fyhtwite’. In H, I Æthelred follows; in B, ‘Ðus man sceal swerigean’ (Schmid's App. X) follows in the same hand without a break, as in Quadr.; AP: corrected against Whitelock p. 430, October 2026 (was “When that has been done, the king’s mund is to be established; 21 days from that day healsfang is to be paid; 21 days from then the compensation to the lord for his man; 21 days from then the first instalment of the wergild.”, now “When that has been done, the king’s mund is to be established; 21 days from that day healsfang is to be paid; 21 days from then the compensation to the lord for his man; 21 days from then the first instalment of the wergild. (expanded letters in italics: mund, healsfang)”)

Cf. Gl Mannbusse 3. It is not the case that the penalty for fighting is contained in it (Steenstrup Danelag 321); rather, it is to be supplied for II Em from Wer, even if it was still lacking in the statement of the law that lay before II Em (see above 7¹), because that statement concerned an arbitration without a fine for the state authority
Cf. Be Wer. 4 and see Pollock, The King’s Peace (Oxford Lectures), p. 77.

Cf. Wi. 11 and note; 12; 14.
In Be Wer. 4, 1 the amount of the healsfang in the case of a wergeld of 1200 shillings is said to be 120 shillings. This is repeated in Hn. 76, 4 b, where the sum is stated both in the old currency and in the Norman currency (50 shillings of 12 pence).
The amount of the ceorl’s healsfang is not stated by any of the earlier authorities but in Hn. 76, 6 a and 7 it is said to be 12/6 in Norman currency which would be 30 shillings in the old currency. Liebermann suggests that this is a mistake, due to confusion with the manbot payable for a ceorl (see In. 70), and seems to incline to the opinion that the healsfang was regularly ⅒ of the wergeld in the case of the ceorl as well as in that of the thegn. He quotes Leis Wl. 8, 1; 9 where the wergeld of the ceorl is said to be 100 shillings, i.e. 1200 pence, both in Mercia and Wessex, and the healsfang of the ceorl to be 10 shillings, i.e. 120 pence, in both regions. But this assessment of the ceorl’s wergeld, if not a mere mistake, is an innovation, as before the Conquest it was 200 shillings, i.e. 800 pence in Mercia and 1000 pence in Wessex. The amount fixed for the healsfang in Leis Wl. 9 would be correct for Mercian custom before the Conquest if reckoned at 30 (Mercian) shillings. Some evidence for the correctness of this amount as the ceorl’s healsfang is perhaps given by the custom of Hereford (see DB. i. 179 a, 1), where the heriot of the burgess is said to be 10 shillings, i.e. 120 pence. In II Cn. 71, 2 the healsfang and the heriot are identified in the case of the ‘medeme þegen’ in Wessex, though no heriot is stated for the ceorl.

note.label: mund
note.seg: “protection.” This clause means that any act of violence after that will be regarded as a breach of the king’s special protection.

note.label: healsfang
note.seg: A part of the wergild which went to the nearest kin. see p. 397, n. 6.

note.label: paid
note.seg: It is possible that the clause “twenty-one days from then the fine for fighting” has been omitted at this point. It occurs in a document of very similar content to much of this code, usually cited as Wergild. Nevertheless, it remains a possibility that an intentional alteration is being made by one of these texts.
